fr:mainmatter.html:p: Once the contract is written in Lean, it is a complete description of what a circuit must do and says nothing about how. Fix the input and output types, the assumptions, the spec, and the exact statements to be proved, and the circuit itself becomes free — any implementation is acceptable if its exported proofs have the right types. Acceptance is then decided by the kernel rather than by review, and the provenance of the circuit stops mattering.

The consequence is for optimisation, which is otherwise the most dangerous change one can make to a circuit. Optimising a circuit means removing constraints, and the failure mode of removing a constraint is not a wrong answer but a permitted wrong answer — invisible to tests, invisible to the honest prover, and beyond the reach of review at the scale of a hash function with hundreds of thousands of rows. Against a machine-checked interface the calculus inverts: an optimisation that breaks soundness fails to compile, so the class of bug that is hardest to find becomes the class that is hardest to ship. The specification is a total function (in contrast to my previous work where a specification is not known to be total, so a reference implementation is treated as a "total" specification).

An interface that fixes only soundness and completeness is not enough for this, and the omissions are instructive. Cost has to be in the interface, or "optimised" is not a measurable claim. The shape of the constraint system has to be fixed too, or the cost number is not comparable between submissions — a submitter who is allowed to write assertions of arbitrary degree can pack several rows into one and report a smaller count. Computability of the witnesses has to be required, or a circuit can satisfy both correctness obligations while no prover can actually run it. And the axioms have to be bounded, since a proof is only as good as what it is allowed to assume. zk.golf pins down all four alongside the spec, and that combination is what makes an arbitrary submission — including a machine-generated one — safe to accept unread.

Whether this generalises past circuits is a separate question, and my own answer is that it generalises less than it looks. The technique works here because the specifications are easy: SHA-256 is a total function on byte strings and the spec is an equation, so writing the interface is bookkeeping. The difficulty with smart contract specifications was never the proof, it was that the properties worth having were socio-economic and resisted statement — and an interface-as-specification discipline would have inherited that difficulty rather than dissolved it. Circuits are the setting where the discipline pays, and the reason is the shape of the specification problem, not the strength of the method.

A competition, run by zkSecurity, to write the cheapest circuit satisfying a fixed formal interface, with correctness proved in Lean using Clean. Each challenge is a directory of Lean files rather than a prose problem statement, and the interesting design decision is which files are trusted. The interface file owns the input and output types, the assumptions, and the spec. The challenge file — described in its own header as the trusted boundary — declares the circuit and the theorems with their bodies left as sorry, so the obligation is exactly to supply terms of those types. A configuration file names the declarations that must be present and the axioms they may depend on. The implementation is unconstrained.

The SHA-256 instance makes the interface concrete. Input is a 256-byte buffer encoded one byte per field element, plus a length; output is the digest as eight 32-bit words. The assumptions are that every buffer entry is a byte and that the length is below the buffer size. The spec is an equation: the digest equals SHA-256 of the first n bytes, where SHA-256 is defined in the challenge repository over the naturals, with padding and compression written out. It is stated as a GeneralFormalCircuit rather than a FormalCircuit, and the reason is precise — the honest prover is additionally required to zero the buffer beyond the message length, which is an obligation on the prover and not an assumption the verifier may make. Coupling the two statements, as the simpler structure does, would have put a padding condition into the soundness theorem.

Five theorems are required, and the three beyond soundness and completeness are the ones that make the score mean anything. Cost is a pair — witness allocations and constraint rows — and the requirement is that the circuit's count equals a declared pair for every input and at every offset, so the number is a property of the circuit rather than the outcome of a benchmark. Because it is a theorem, a submitted score is certified rather than measured.

The second, isR1CS, fixes the shape of the constraint system. A single row is an asserted expression in which, along the addition spine, every summand is affine and at most one is a product of two affine forms — the shape A \cdot B - C, one rank-one constraint \langle A, z \rangle \cdot \langle B, z \rangle = \langle C, z \rangle . Degree three and above is rejected, and so is a sum of two products, which genuinely needs an auxiliary witness and a second row. The check is documented as a sound over-approximation: it counts products syntactically, so it can over-reject — ab + ac is rank one but counts as two — and never under-counts, which is the direction that matters, because a true multi-row assertion is never certified as one row. Lookups and channel interactions are forbidden outright.

That prohibition is what shapes every number in the competition. With no lookups, bitwise operations are bit-blasted: in the published SHA-256 solution a 32-bit XOR costs 32 allocations and 32 constraints, a 32-bit addition 33 and 34, and the majority function 64 of each. One round is two \Sigma functions, a choice, a majority, and seven additions — 455 allocations and 462 constraints. Sixty-four rounds, the message schedule, and the feed-forward addition make one block cost 40,280 and 40,880; five blocks with the padding checks and digest selection give the interface total, 204,224 allocations and 209,586 constraints. A single 256-byte SHA-256 therefore scores 413,810, on the convention that the score is the sum of the two — and the same accounting puts a Keccak permutation at 153,600 of each, a 4096-bit RSA-with-SHA-256 signature check at 412,130 and 415,006, and a secp256k1 scalar multiplication above eight million of each.

The third theorem, computableWitness, requires that every witness generator depend only on the circuit's input and on cells already allocated. This is the obligation that keeps the other four honest. Nothing in soundness or completeness prevents a generator from reading a cell it has not yet assigned, or from being defined by a non-executable choice; a circuit with such a generator can be correct on both counts and still be one no prover can run. Requiring the property as a theorem is how the interface says runnable without saying anything about the implementation.

Validation is then mechanical, and deliberately so. The submission must typecheck against the declared types, and its axiom dependencies must stay inside a whitelist — propositional extensionality, quotient soundness, classical choice, and, per instance, the assertion that the target prime is prime, which is asserted rather than proved because checking it in the kernel is expensive. There is a flag for re-checking with an independent kernel implementation, currently off. Nothing in the pipeline reads the circuit. zkSecurity's own framing of why this matters is that frontier models can now produce deeply optimised circuits with proofs in days; I cannot check that claim from the repository, but it is not the load-bearing one. The structural point is that the interface makes the question of who wrote the circuit irrelevant to whether it can be accepted, and a competition is a clean way to demonstrate it.

Sources: the zk-golf-challenges repository, read at the initial public-challenge commit — Challenge/Instances/SHA256 for the interface and the trusted boundary, Challenge/Utils/CostR1CS.lean for the cost and rank-one certification, configs/ for the axiom whitelists, and Solution/ for the published reference circuits and their costs; zk.golf and Fearless and Collaborative Optimization of Circuits for the competition's own account of scoring, which I have not read directly.

fr:title.text: Clean: Circuits and Their Specifications in Lean

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Clean: Circuits and Their Specifications in Lean

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An embedded Lean DSL for writing zk circuits against AIR, Plonkish, and R1CS, built by zkSecurity under a Verified-zkEVM grant. Circuit, specification, and proof live in the same file. The constraints of such a circuit cut out an algebraic variety in the witness cells: a satisfying assignment is a point on that variety, and the spec is what that point is supposed to mean.

The object that carries the correctness claim is FormalCircuit, and its content is a contract. A circuit is bundled with an Assumptions predicate on its inputs, a Spec relating inputs to outputs, and proofs of two statements: soundness, that the constraints together with the assumptions imply the spec, and completeness, that the assumptions imply the circuit's own witness generators satisfy the constraints. Taken together they say the circuit behaves as a function with Assumptions as precondition and Spec as postcondition.

What makes the arrangement scale is that subcircuits enter proofs through their specs rather than their constraints. ConstraintsHold.Soundness replaces each subcircuit in the operation list by the implication from its assumptions to its spec, and the completeness counterpart replaces it by its prover-side assumptions — so a gadget is proved once and thereafter used as a black box. The 200,000-constraint SHA-256 circuit in the zk.golf repository is proved this way, as a composition of some twenty gadget circuits each carrying its own soundness and completeness theorem, none of them reproved at the top level.

Clean and ArkLib prove complementary halves of a proof system's correctness and do not currently compose (but may do in the future). ArkLib's theorems are about a protocol over a constraint system: given that the system is satisfiable, the argument is knowledge-sound. Clean's theorems are about what satisfiability of that system means for the computation. The protocol theorem assumes the arithmetisation says what it is meant to say, and the circuit theorem is what discharges that assumption — but joining them is an exploratory item on Clean's roadmap, not a result. This is the load-bearing seam between the two libraries, and it is still open.

A Circuit F α in Clean is a function from an offset to a value and a list of operations — ℕ → α × List (Operation F) — which is a writer monad accumulating operations mixed with a state monad threading the offset. The offset is the index of the next unallocated witness cell, and bind advances it by the number of cells the preceding operations allocated. That is the whole of the representation, and the do notation is what makes it readable: a circuit is written as a straight-line program that allocates cells and asserts equations, and the monad turns it into a list.

There are five operations. witness m ir allocates m cells and records how to compute them; assert e requires the expression e to vanish; lookup requires a row to appear in a table; interact emits a channel interaction; subcircuit nests an already-proved circuit. Only three of the five are checked by the verifier. witness carries no constraint whatsoever — it is instruction to the prover, invisible in the constraint system.

That asymmetry is where circuit bugs live. A circuit is two programs sharing one syntax: the constraint system the verifier checks, and the witness generator the prover runs. An under-constrained circuit is one whose generator computes the right value and whose constraints also permit a wrong one, and no amount of testing finds it, because testing runs the generator. Clean's response is to state soundness over the constraints alone, with the generator appearing only in the completeness statement — so the property that testing cannot reach is the property the soundness proof is about.

Expressions are a small inductive type — variable, constant, addition, multiplication — so an Expression F is a polynomial in the witness cells, and assertZero is the only primitive constraint. Two pieces of notation cover most circuit code: x === y asserts an equality, and let b <== e allocates a cell and constrains it equal to e, which is the idiom for naming an intermediate value that the verifier can refer to.

Witness generation is written in a deep-embedded IR rather than as a Lean closure, and the reason is that the prover does not run in Lean. Because WitgenIR is data it can be serialised to a proving backend, checked for exportability, and still evaluated inside Lean by a reference interpreter, so one definition serves the proof and the Rust prover both. The authoring surface has two sorts: field-sorted expressions with +, \times and inverse, and a 64-bit integer sort with wrapping arithmetic and bitwise operations, plus conditionals, comparisons, and bit extraction. Gadgets work on bytes and 32-bit limbs, so the wraps are never taken, and the normalisation simproc erases them whenever the gadget's own assumptions bound the operand. Anything genuinely wider than 64 bits has to stay field-sorted.

Two supporting classes make gadgets composable. ProvableType equips a type former with a size, maps to and from a flat vector of that many elements, and round-trip proofs — this is how a structured input becomes a run of witness cells, and record types get it by deriving ProvableStruct. ElaboratedCircuit carries the offset-independent facts about a circuit: how many cells it allocates and what it outputs, each with a proof that it agrees with actually running the circuit. Elaboration is what lets a caller use a gadget without unfolding its body, and it is inferred by tactic in the common case.

fr:title.text: Soundness and Completeness of a Circuit

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Soundness and Completeness of a Circuit

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Circuit soundness and protocol soundness are statements about different objects, and the distinction is worth holding onto because both are called soundness. A protocol theorem says that a prover who convinces the verifier knows a satisfying assignment to some constraint system. A circuit theorem says what a satisfying assignment to that system implies about the computation the system was supposed to encode. Neither implies the other, and a proof system with both is the only kind whose end-to-end claim mentions the program the user cared about.

Soundness in Clean quantifies over arbitrary environments. For every offset, every assignment of field elements to cells — no honesty assumed — and every input, if the assumptions hold on the input and the constraints hold under that assignment, then the spec holds of the input and the circuit's output. Quantifying over all environments is what makes this a statement about a cheating prover: the witness cells are adversarial, and the constraints are the only thing the proof has to work with.

Completeness quantifies over prover environments that use the circuit's own witness generators — the predicate UsesLocalWitnessesCompleteness says the environment's cells agree, operation by operation, with what each witness step computes. Given assumptions, the constraints hold. So completeness is exactly the claim that the generator's output satisfies the constraints on every admissible input, and it is the obligation that fails when a circuit is over-constrained rather than under-constrained. The proof obligation splits differently at subcircuits too: soundness may assume a subcircuit's spec, while completeness must establish its prover-side assumptions.

Three structures package the pair, and the differences between them are the interesting part of the design. FormalCircuit is the function-like case: a spec relating input to output, and constraints that are always satisfiable given the assumptions, so the spec is permitted to be strictly weaker than the constraints. FormalAssertion is the case with no output, where the circuit's purpose is to constrain its input further. Its constraints need not be satisfiable, so completeness is weakened to assumptions and spec imply constraints — and the consequence is that an assertion's spec must be an equivalent reformulation of its constraints, not a weakening of them.

GeneralFormalCircuit is for circuits that are a mix of the two, and it decouples the statements outright: Assumptions and Spec appear only in soundness, and separate ProverAssumptions and ProverSpec only in completeness. The library's own motivating example is the bit-decomposition gadget. Decomposing x into n bits constrains x to be n-bit representable as a side effect, so representability is a necessary assumption for completeness and an unnecessary one for soundness. Stating it as a FormalCircuit would push the assumption into the soundness statement and make the gadget useless as a range check, because it would then require the very property it establishes. A fourth structure, DeterministicFormalCircuit, adds a uniqueness obligation: the spec determines the output, so the constraints cannot leave it ambiguous.

Soundness carries a second conjunct that is easy to overlook. Alongside the spec, the circuit must discharge the Requirements of every channel interaction it emits — the obligations a component takes on when it pushes to a channel, as opposed to the guarantees it may assume when it pulls. At the level of a single circuit these are assumed and re-exported; establishing them unconditionally is a property of the whole ensemble, and it does not follow from the circuit-level proofs.

What is not yet stated anywhere in this stack is the composite theorem. Completeness at the protocol layer is preserved by compilation and is rarely where a system fails; circuit completeness is a different obligation, and the flat AIR ensemble layer marks it as unproved. Until circuit-level and protocol-level statements are joined, a verified circuit and a verified argument are two theorems about the same system with a gap between them, and the gap is exactly the arithmetisation's satisfiability relation.

Clean advertises AIR, Plonkish, and R1CS, and the three are not supported to the same depth. AIR is the one that is built out: Clean.Air is a row-oriented layer with components, tables, channels, and ensembles, and the plonky3 backend carries a Clean circuit through to an actual plonky3 proof. Plonkish support in the sense of custom gates is a roadmap item. R1CS has no backend at all — and the largest R1CS circuits written in Clean get their arithmetisation guarantee from outside the library, through the zk.golf challenge harness, which certifies by a Lean predicate that every assertion in a circuit is a single rank-one row. That is a reasonable division of labour, but it means "targets R1CS" currently describes a property provable about Clean circuits rather than a compilation path out of them.

The AIR style Clean models is flat AIR: one circuit checked independently on each row, with no reference to adjacent rows. Everything that would classically be a next-row constraint — a VM state transition, a lookup, a link to a public API — is expressed as a channel interaction instead, and correctness comes from those interactions balancing across the whole table ensemble. This matches how modern zkVMs are actually laid out, and it is the reason the circuit-level obligations include channel requirements. A Flat.Component is a one-row component backed by a GeneralFormalCircuit; a Flat.Table is a concrete trace for one component together with its prover data.

An ensemble is components, channels, and a verifier circuit, and its statement is the raw relation a proof system proves: there exists a witness whose table constraints hold and whose channel interactions balance. Ensemble soundness is not a lifting of circuit soundness, and this is the sharpest point in the layer. Local circuit proofs assume the guarantees on the channels they pull from; the ensemble argument has to establish those unconditionally, from global balance plus the constraints. Clean gives two arguments for two channel disciplines. Ordinary lookup-like channels are handled by a hierarchy condition — every table that pushes to a channel precedes every table that pulls from it — via a relaxed notion of balance that tolerates interactions from tables added later, which is what makes the argument inductive. VM-like components cannot satisfy that condition, since they both pull from and push to the same state channel, so they get a dedicated theorem resting on a reversal of guarantees and requirements. Ensemble completeness is marked TODO.

An older table layer coexists with this one. Clean/Table models classic AIRs where a transition relates adjacent rows directly, by placing the output of one step in the same relative position as the input of the next, and the Fibonacci and Keccak inductive tables are written against it. The two layers are independent for now, with the flat one intended to absorb the other.

The plonky3 backend is a proof of concept by its own description, not a production path: it imports a Clean circuit as a plonky3 AIR, generates the trace, and proves it, demonstrated on the Fibonacci table. What is missing from the picture — and it is the more consequential gap — is verifier challenges. Clean has no model of them yet, so lookup arguments are not proved end to end inside the library: a lookup operation is an assumption of the circuit layer, discharged either by the channel balance theory above or, in a deployed system, by the backend and nothing in Lean. Lookups are where a modern zkVM's prover time goes, so this is the part of the stack where the formalisation is furthest from the engineering.

The zero-test is the gadget worth reading first, because it is four lines long and every feature of the contract is visible in it. Witness a cell z to be x^{-1} when x \neq 0 and 0 otherwise; constrain b = 1 - xz; assert bx = 0; return b. The spec is that b = 1 when x = 0 and b = 0 otherwise, and both proofs go through by a single tactic call.

Soundness reads off the two constraints without reference to the generator. If x = 0 then b = 1 - 0 = 1. If x 
eq 0 then bx = 0 forces b = 0. Nothing about z was used, which is the point — z is adversarial. Completeness is the other direction and does use the generator: at x 
eq 0 the choice z = x^{-1} gives b = 1 - 1 = 0, so bx = 0 holds. Now delete the assertion bx = 0. The circuit is still complete, because the honest generator still produces b = 0 at x 
eq 0; it is no longer sound, because a prover may set z = 0, obtain b = 1, and claim a nonzero x is zero. That is the whole under-constraining failure mode in four lines, and the reason the two obligations are proved separately.

A field inverse is a witness rather than a constraint because the constraint language has no division, and this is the standard trick everywhere in circuit engineering. What the specification adds is a check on the trick: the equality b = 1 - xz is not obviously a zero-test, and the theorem is what says it is one.

Byte addition shows where assumptions come from. The gadget assumes both inputs are below 256 and specifies that the output is their sum modulo 256, and it is built as a thin wrapper around an add-with-carry gadget, whose own proofs discharge both obligations by simplification. The assumption is load-bearing in a way that has nothing to do with bytes: the gadget is stated over a prime field with the hypothesis p > 512, so that x + y + c \leq 511 cannot wrap the field before it wraps 256. Drop the range assumption and the spec becomes false, not merely unprovable — the arithmetic being modelled is 256-modular only inside a window the field is large enough to contain.

Tables are where a gadget's spec gets consumed by something larger. The 8-bit Fibonacci table has rows of two field elements; its two-row constraint copies the current row's second value into the next row's first, calls the byte-addition gadget for the next row's second, and a boundary constraint pins row zero to (0, 1). The table's spec is a statement about the whole trace — at every index i the row holds \mathrm {fib}(i) and \mathrm {fib}(i+1) reduced modulo 256 — and the proof of it consumes the addition gadget's spec, never its constraints. That is the same modularity as at the circuit level, one layer up.

The gadget library is mostly what a hash function needs: byte and 32-bit addition, rotation on 32- and 64-bit words, the bitwise operations, boolean and bit decomposition, equality and zero tests, conditional selection — and on top of them SHA-256, Keccak, and BLAKE3 as complete gadgets, with Keccak also available as an inductive table. There is also a port of circomlib into Clean, which is a good instinct: verifying the gadgets the ecosystem already depends on tests the library against circuits whose intended behaviour is settled and whose bugs, if any, matter today.

Alongside the circuits sits a directory of reference semantics — SHA-256, Keccak-256, Poseidon, BLAKE3 — written in Lean over the naturals, and next to those, Python implementations of SHA-256 and Keccak. The Python is there to cross-check the Lean spec against a known-good implementation, which is the computable specification argument in miniature. The soundness theorem relates a circuit to a spec, and gives no information about whether the spec is the hash function; running the spec on the standard test vectors is the only thing that does.

fr:title.text: A Note on Clean and Circuit Specifications

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A Note on Clean and Circuit Specifications

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Clean is now written out as a section of the zkVMs and SNARKs corpus, from the sources rather than from the announcements. The claim it organises around is that a circuit specification is a contract — assumptions as precondition, spec as postcondition — and that the two halves of it have to be proved separately, because each is satisfiable on its own by a circuit that is useless in the opposite direction. What convinced me the framing is more than tidy bookkeeping is zk.golf, where the contract is fixed in Lean and the circuit is left entirely free, so an optimised circuit is accepted or rejected by the kernel and never by review. That works for a hash function because the specification is an equation; it would not have rescued the smart contract specifications I spent a thesis on, and the difference is in the specification problem rather than in the method.

The pages:
Circuits, constraints, and witness generation — the circuit monad, the five operations, and why witness generation is compiled to a serialisable IR rather than written as a Lean closure.
Soundness and completeness of a circuit — the two obligations stated precisely, and what the three circuit structures are for. The bit-decomposition gadget is the example that forces the general form.
Arithmetisations and backends — flat AIR, channels and ensembles, and an honest accounting of how deep the AIR, Plonkish, and R1CS support actually goes.
Circuits in Clean — the zero-test read line by line, including what breaks when one constraint is deleted, plus byte addition and the Fibonacci table.
Algebraic varieties — a Clean circuit's constraints cut out a variety; the spec is what that variety is supposed to mean.
Interfaces as specifications — what an interface has to pin down beyond soundness and completeness, and zk.golf as the worked case, with the SHA-256 cost broken down.

Two things are open and worth naming. Clean and ArkLib prove complementary halves of a proof system's correctness and do not compose — joining them is an exploratory roadmap item, and until it happens a verified circuit and a verified argument are two theorems with the arithmetisation's satisfiability relation between them. And verifier challenges are not modelled, so lookup arguments are not proved end to end inside Clean, which is awkward given that lookups are where a zkVM's prover time goes.

fr:title.text: Proof Assistants and the Issue of Incorrect Specification

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Proof Assistants and the Issue of Incorrect Specification

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Proof assistants give us a formal and robustly mathematical environment in which to prove mathematical theorems and arbitrary properties of programs. Virtually anything that can be stated; true propositions can all in principle be proved. You would think that this would make proof assistants the silver bullet to software security: Since you could truly state and prove any desirable security or performance property, if the tools are good enough you might think that they are precisely what's needed to make high-assurance software absolutely bullet-proof. The reality is, however, it is difficult to write a complete specification; desirable properties of some software can be extremely difficult to articulate.

Some software will need a great deal of formal infrastructure built up to write provably correct specifications. For others, it's not even obvious that formal statements are the right tool to use for them. Computer science has a long history of using diagrams, pictures, and other tools of abstraction to specify computation. Maybe a proof assistant is powerful enough to formalize any abstract framework? Maybe it's powerful enough to do this? If it is, how do we proceed? How do we coax that power out so that all desirable properties of software can be clearly articulated, specified and ultimately formally proved? Circuits are the case where the answer is plainly yes, and the reason is that their desirable properties are already equations rather than something that has to be coaxed into formal shape.
Smart contracts can have deceptively difficult specifications.

Dexter2 is an AMM on the Tezos blockchain that has been formally verified by at least three different groups using three different formal verification tools. Each was based on the same informal specification. The informal specification describes the contract interface, including its entrypoint functions, error messages, outgoing transactions, the contents of its storage, some invariants of the storage (including that its store of tokens never fully depletes), fees, and the logic of each of the entrypoint functions. This is a standard and detailed contract specification.

However, while the specification is detailed on the contract design and interface, it doesn’t include anything about expected or desired behavior from an economic perspective. This is not because the expected or desired economic behavior is unknown or uninteresting. It was clearly articulated by Vitalik Buterin, co-founder of Ethereum, in what he wrote in March 2018 about AMMs on the online forum Ethereum Research. Buterin proposed that AMMs trade between a pair of tokens along an indifference curve:

where x represents the quantity held by the contract of the token being traded in, y represents the quantity held by the contract of the token being traded out, and k is a constant. The tokens held by the contract come from liquidity providers, which are investors who deposit tokens into the AMM in exchange for a reward, most often a share of transaction fees. That k is constant means that a trade of \Delta x of one token yields \Delta y of another such that the product from above stays constant at k:

Buterin argued that an AMM that trades along this indifference curve features efficient price discovery. He also argued that it can properly incentivize liquidity providers by charging a 0.3% fee on each trade to give to them.

We can probably convince ourselves that the informal specification of Dexter2 features these economic qualities described by Buterin, including efficient price discovery and some suitable incentive mechanism so that investors deposit tokens into the AMM contract and provide liquidity to the market; however, concluding that the informal specification or its formal counterparts actually imply any of these economic behaviors is not a given fact. AMM fees and liquidity provision alone are highly complex topics, and are the subject of several economic studies, including on choosing optimal transaction fees, how liquidity providers react to market changes, and how all of that relates to the curvature of the indifference curve xy= k. It was also shown that front-running attacks can warp the incentive scheme of the blockchain itself in such a way that could compromise its underlying security.

There is then an outstanding question of whether any of Dexter2’s specifications are correct with regards to the desired—indeed, essential—high-level economic and game-theoretic behavior of the resulting AMM. Not only do these important economic and game-theoretic factors not make it into any of Dexter2’s specifications, formal or informal, but to complicate matters a brief study of the three formalizations of Dexter2’s informal specification reveals that each differs substantively both in how the properties of the informal specification are formalized, and in what assumptions are made in the process of verification.

Furthermore, were we to try to formally specify some of the aforementioned high-level economic and game-theoretic behaviors on the Dexter2 contract it is not at all obvious how we would go about doing so. Most specification languages and models of computation are too low-level to easily admit clear specifications of such properties. What model or framework would we use, for example, to specify that Dexter2 facilitate an efficient market?

As codebases go, Dexter2 is quite small—only a few thousand lines—but as we’ve seen much is expected of it in terms of its economic and game-theoretic behavior; because AMMs like Dexter2 routinely manage billions of USD worth of funds, much is also at risk in case of a bug. Furthermore, despite the fact that they are not present in any of Dexter2’s specifications, it is difficult to conceptualize a notion of Dexter2’s correctness that does not include some of the economic properties that we have just mentioned, directly or indirectly. It is, however, not obvious that these properties hold by reading any of the aforementioned specifications.

The problem that Dexter2 illustrates is that smart contracts have social, game theoretic, and crypto-economic properties that are difficult to state in a prose specification, much less in a formal way. This in contrast with something like ZK circuits, which are an interesting, contrasting case: a hash function's specification is an equation, so fixing an interface in Lean is enough to make optimisation safe — a discipline that would have bought nothing here.

fr:title.text: Smart Contract Vulnerabilities Due to Poor Specification

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Smart Contract Vulnerabilities Due to Poor Specification

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Smart contracts are vulnerable due to incorrect code, but equally due to incorrect specification (or design). There are more examples of this that can possibly be included here, but I have written up a few examples. We would recognize each of these exploits as attacks, despite the fact that the contracts were functioning as specified, which tells us that the specifications were erroneous as they did not accurately capture the intended economic behaviors. To the contrary, they permitted unintended and pathological behavior.

Beanstalk is (was) an Ethereum-based stablecoin protocol which uses a decentralized governance protocol. This governance protocol features an emergency commit function, which gives a supermajority of governance votes power to quickly respond to an emergency by approving and executing a proposal in one single vote. The goal of said emergency commit function is to allow governance to respond quickly to an emergency, providing added security in the face of unforeseen vulnerabilities.

In a turn of grim irony, this very emergency response mechanism turned out to be the source of a catastrophic exploit. On April 17, 2022, an attacker used a flash loan to temporarily buy a supermajority of governance tokens and execute a proposal, draining the contract of approximately 77 million USD in lost contract assets A flash loan is a loan mediated by a smart contract and issued for the duration of a single, atomic transaction. Due to its atomicity, a flash loan removes the creditor’s risk of debt default, and thus enables enormous, uncollateralized loans. For example, the Aave flash loan pool has had in excess of 1 billion USD which can be loaned out. Flash loans can introduce unintuitive contract behavior, deviating from that of traditional markets. Importantly, the Beanstalk attack leveraged the unexpected behavior due to the availability of flash loans, exploiting the faulty design of the governance mechanism rather than incorrect code.

fr:title.text: Spartan Protocol and Pancake Bunny Hack (2021)

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Spartan Protocol and Pancake Bunny Hack (2021)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: More examples of successful flash loan attacks include attacks on the Spartan Protocol and Pancake Bunny, two DeFi contracts on the Binance Smart Chain (BSC). Attackers used flash loans to make huge trades and temporarily manipulate market prices of certain assets. Both of these contracts used these market prices in the contract logic, and in both cases this lead to pathological—though, again, correct according to the flawed specification—contract behavior. In May 2021, an attacker drained the Spartan Protocol contract for a profit of roughly the equivalent of 30 million USD. Another attacker drained Pancake Bunny of 114k WBNB and 697k BUNNY tokens, amounting to about 45 million USD at the time in lost funds.

Finally, Mango Markets, a Solana-based DEX, was attacked in October 2022 for approximately 116 million USD in contract assets. The attack consisted of a complicated and subtle trading strategy which only a sophisticated trader would be able to see and exploit. CoinDesk reported that the attacker did everything within the parameters of the platform’s design. Avraham Eisenberg, the attacker, wrote:

html:p.html:em: "I believe all of our actions were legal open market actions, using the protocol as designed, even if the development team did not fully anticipate all the consequences of setting parameters the way they are."

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Nomad is (was) a cross-chain bridge protocol. In August 2022, more than 500 hacker addresses exploited a bug introduced by a faulty upgrade to one of the Nomad smart contracts. The upgrade incorrectly added the null address (0x000...000) as a trusted root, which turned off a key safety check, allowing anyone to withdraw arbitrary amounts of funds from the Nomad contract to their wallet by calling the contract with a particular payload. The attack resulted in 190 million USD in lost funds.

Similarly, Uranium Finance, an AMM, suffered a costly exploit after a faulty contract upgrade. The original contract contained a constant, k, equal to 1_000 in three different places, which was used to price trades. The update changed this value to 10_000 in two places but not the third, presumably to calculate trades with higher precision. The result of this was that the attacker could swap virtually nothing in for 98% of the total balance of any output token, which resulted in a loss of 50 million USD of contract funds. NowSwap, a nearly identical application, upgraded with the same error and incurred a loss of 1 million USD.

A competition, run by zkSecurity, to write the cheapest circuit satisfying a fixed formal interface, with correctness proved in Lean using Clean. Each challenge is a directory of Lean files rather than a prose problem statement, and the interesting design decision is which files are trusted. The interface file owns the input and output types, the assumptions, and the spec. The challenge file — described in its own header as the trusted boundary — declares the circuit and the theorems with their bodies left as sorry, so the obligation is exactly to supply terms of those types. A configuration file names the declarations that must be present and the axioms they may depend on. The implementation is unconstrained.

The SHA-256 instance makes the interface concrete. Input is a 256-byte buffer encoded one byte per field element, plus a length; output is the digest as eight 32-bit words. The assumptions are that every buffer entry is a byte and that the length is below the buffer size. The spec is an equation: the digest equals SHA-256 of the first n bytes, where SHA-256 is defined in the challenge repository over the naturals, with padding and compression written out. It is stated as a GeneralFormalCircuit rather than a FormalCircuit, and the reason is precise — the honest prover is additionally required to zero the buffer beyond the message length, which is an obligation on the prover and not an assumption the verifier may make. Coupling the two statements, as the simpler structure does, would have put a padding condition into the soundness theorem.

Five theorems are required, and the three beyond soundness and completeness are the ones that make the score mean anything. Cost is a pair — witness allocations and constraint rows — and the requirement is that the circuit's count equals a declared pair for every input and at every offset, so the number is a property of the circuit rather than the outcome of a benchmark. Because it is a theorem, a submitted score is certified rather than measured.

The second, isR1CS, fixes the shape of the constraint system. A single row is an asserted expression in which, along the addition spine, every summand is affine and at most one is a product of two affine forms — the shape A \cdot B - C, one rank-one constraint \langle A, z \rangle \cdot \langle B, z \rangle = \langle C, z \rangle . Degree three and above is rejected, and so is a sum of two products, which genuinely needs an auxiliary witness and a second row. The check is documented as a sound over-approximation: it counts products syntactically, so it can over-reject — ab + ac is rank one but counts as two — and never under-counts, which is the direction that matters, because a true multi-row assertion is never certified as one row. Lookups and channel interactions are forbidden outright.

That prohibition is what shapes every number in the competition. With no lookups, bitwise operations are bit-blasted: in the published SHA-256 solution a 32-bit XOR costs 32 allocations and 32 constraints, a 32-bit addition 33 and 34, and the majority function 64 of each. One round is two \Sigma functions, a choice, a majority, and seven additions — 455 allocations and 462 constraints. Sixty-four rounds, the message schedule, and the feed-forward addition make one block cost 40,280 and 40,880; five blocks with the padding checks and digest selection give the interface total, 204,224 allocations and 209,586 constraints. A single 256-byte SHA-256 therefore scores 413,810, on the convention that the score is the sum of the two — and the same accounting puts a Keccak permutation at 153,600 of each, a 4096-bit RSA-with-SHA-256 signature check at 412,130 and 415,006, and a secp256k1 scalar multiplication above eight million of each.

The third theorem, computableWitness, requires that every witness generator depend only on the circuit's input and on cells already allocated. This is the obligation that keeps the other four honest. Nothing in soundness or completeness prevents a generator from reading a cell it has not yet assigned, or from being defined by a non-executable choice; a circuit with such a generator can be correct on both counts and still be one no prover can run. Requiring the property as a theorem is how the interface says runnable without saying anything about the implementation.

Validation is then mechanical, and deliberately so. The submission must typecheck against the declared types, and its axiom dependencies must stay inside a whitelist — propositional extensionality, quotient soundness, classical choice, and, per instance, the assertion that the target prime is prime, which is asserted rather than proved because checking it in the kernel is expensive. There is a flag for re-checking with an independent kernel implementation, currently off. Nothing in the pipeline reads the circuit. zkSecurity's own framing of why this matters is that frontier models can now produce deeply optimised circuits with proofs in days; I cannot check that claim from the repository, but it is not the load-bearing one. The structural point is that the interface makes the question of who wrote the circuit irrelevant to whether it can be accepted, and a competition is a clean way to demonstrate it.

Sources: the zk-golf-challenges repository, read at the initial public-challenge commit — Challenge/Instances/SHA256 for the interface and the trusted boundary, Challenge/Utils/CostR1CS.lean for the cost and rank-one certification, configs/ for the axiom whitelists, and Solution/ for the published reference circuits and their costs; zk.golf and Fearless and Collaborative Optimization of Circuits for the competition's own account of scoring, which I have not read directly.

fr:title.text: Formally Specifying Contract Optimizations With Bisimulations in Coq

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Formally Specifying Contract Optimizations With Bisimulations in Coq

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Paper Abstract: The efficacy of formal verification of smart contracts depends on being able to correctly specify and carry out the verification of optimized code. However, code optimized for performance is rarely optimized for intelligibility, which can make formally verifying optimized code difficult and costly. To address this issue, we present a formal tool for reasoning about an optimized contract in terms of its reference implementation. This tool reduces the work of formally verifying an optimized contract to proving behavioral equivalence to the reference implementation.
